en: *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle. Extracted from the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Precepts" (*Bhūmi-vyavasthāna-śīla-paṭala*) spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Translated at Guzang by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema of India during the Northern Liang dynasty.
I take refuge in Vairocana and the Vajra Buddhas of the ten directions;
I also pay homage to the former masters of the treatise and the Honored One Maitreya who shall awaken.
Now I shall expound the three clusters of precepts; may all Bodhisattvas listen together.
Precepts are like a great bright lamp, capable of dispelling the darkness of the long night;
Precepts are like a true jewel mirror, illuminating all phenomena without exception;
Precepts are like a maṇi jewel, raining down things to relieve poverty and destitution.
"Leaving this world, one swiftly attains Buddhahood; this Dharma alone is supreme!
Therefore, all Bodhisattvas should diligently protect and uphold it. O Great Beings!"
These four *pārājika* dharmas are the *bodhisattva-mātṛkā*, spoken in their entirety.
"If a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and profit, praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is called the first *pārājika* offense."

"If a bodhisattva, possessing personal wealth, out of a nature of stinginess and attachment, fails to give rise to a heart of compassion toward impoverished and suffering sentient beings who have come seeking aid, and thus does not bestow what they seek;
or if there are those who wish to hear the Dharma, yet out of parsimony refuses to speak it—this is called the second *pārājika* offense."

"If a bodhisattva, out of anger, utters harsh and evil words and their mind does not cease; they further strike with their hands, or employ sticks and stones, inflicting injury and terror, such that their hatred increases;
and when the offender seeks repentance, they do not accept the confession but harbors resentment and refuses to let it go—this is called the third *pārājika* offense."

"If a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, teaches counterfeit dharmas, and zealously establishes counterfeit dharmas—whether understanding them through his own mind or receiving them from another—this is called the fourth offense involving defeat (pārājika-sthānīya-dharma)."
“O Great Beings! The four *pārājika* dharmas have already been explained.
If a bodhisattva, having given rise to intense afflictions, commits any one of these offenses, he loses the bodhisattva precepts and must receive them again.”
"Now I ask the great beings:
Is it pure in this regard?
(This is asked) three times.
“O Great Beings! Since there is purity herein, as indicated by your silence,
let this matter be thus upheld!”
“O Great Beings! These numerous *duṣkṛta* (offenses) of a bodhisattva are explained collectively in the Bodhisattva-mātṛkā.

If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), for the duration of one day and night—whether the Buddha is present in the world, or at his stūpas and temples, or regarding the Dharma, or the sūtras, or the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, or the Bodhisattva-mātṛka-piṭaka, or the community of bhikṣus, or the assembly of great bodhisattvas in the worlds of the ten directions;”

If one does not make offerings, whether few or many, nor even perform a single prostration, nor even praise the merits of the Triple Gem with a single verse, nor even manage to purify the mind for a single moment, this is called a transgression of many offenses;
if it is due to a lack of respect, or negligence, or laziness, the transgression arises from defilement;
if it is due to forgetfulness or error, the transgression does not arise from defilement.

There is no offense for a Bodhisattva who has entered the stage of the pure mind, just as a monk who has attained indestructible purity constantly makes offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha according to the established rule.
"If a Bodhisattva is full of desire, lacks contentment, and greedily clings to wealth and goods, this is called a transgression involving many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement."
There is no offense in the following cases:
when, for the sake of severing those [afflictions], one generates the desire and employs skillful means to adopt their antidotes;
yet, because the afflictions are by nature sharp, they arise again and again.
"If a bodhisattva, seeing an elder endowed with virtue, should fail to respect their fellow practitioners;
if out of arrogance or resentment, they do not give rise to reverence and do not yield their seat;
and if, when questioned or invited to teach the Dharma, they fail to respond at all—this is called a transgression of many offenses, a transgression arising from defilement."
If one falls into indolence, if the mind is neutral (*avyākṛta*), or if there is forgetfulness or error, the offense arises from non-affliction. There is no offense in the following cases:

if one has a serious illness, if the mind is distracted, if one is asleep but perceives oneself as awake, or if one does not answer when being questioned or requested for the Dharma—these are called non-offenses.
If the Elder is preaching the Dharma or engaging in definitive discussion;
if one is oneself preaching the Dharma, listening to the Dharma, or engaging in definitive discussion;
or if one is within an assembly for preaching the Dharma or an assembly for definitive discussion—failing to pay homage in these cases does not constitute an offense.
If one protects the mind of the speaker;
if one employs skillful means to subdue them so that they abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome dharmas;
or if one protects the regulations of the Saṃgha.
If it is for the sake of protecting the minds of many people:

"If a bodhisattva, when invited by a donor—whether to their own home, to a monastery, or to another's house—and offered clothing, food, or various requisites, should refuse to accept them or fail to go because of a mind of anger or pride, this is called a transgression of the many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement."
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill, if one lacks strength, if one is insane;
or if one is in a distant location, or if there is danger and difficulty on the road.
If one knows that by not accepting [the invitation], the other will be disciplined, abandoning evil and abiding in goodness;
or if one has previously accepted the invitation;
or if one is practicing wholesome dharmas and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment; or if one desires to hear unprecedented teachings, their beneficial meanings, and definitive discourses.
If one knows that the requester acts out of deceit or malice;
if one protects many people from a mind of resentment;
or if one upholds the regulations of the Sangha.

"If a bodhisattva has a donor who offers various precious objects—gold, silver, pearls, mani-jewels, lapis lazuli, and so forth—and the bodhisattva, out of anger or pride, rejects them in opposition, this is called an offense of many transgressions; it is an offense arising from affliction."
Because of abandoning sentient beings.
If one falls into indolence through negligence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one is insane;
if one knows that upon receiving it, greed and attachment will certainly arise;
or if one knows that upon receiving it, the donor will feel regret.
If one knows that after receiving [the gift], the donor will give rise to delusion;
or if one knows that after receiving it, the donor will suffer from poverty and distress;
or if one knows that this object has been dedicated to the Three Jewels;
If one knows that this object was obtained through robbery;
or if one knows that after receiving it, one will experience much suffering—namely, execution, imprisonment, banishment, punishment, confiscation of property, and censure.

"If a bodhisattva, when sentient beings come to him desiring to hear the Dharma, out of a nature of malice, resentment, or envy, does not preach it for them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction."
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense in the following cases:
if it is an outsider seeking a shortcoming; or...
If one has a serious illness; if one is insane;
if one knows that by not speaking [the truth] one will bring the other person to discipline;
or if the practice one is cultivating has not yet been mastered.
If one knows that the person before them is unable to show respect and compliance;
if their deportment is disordered;
or if they are of dull faculties and would give rise to a mind of fear upon hearing the profound and wondrous Dharma;
If one knows that after hearing it, wrong views will increase;
if one knows that after hearing it, they will disparage and fall away from it;
or if one knows that after hearing it, they will speak of it to evil people.

"If a bodhisattva, with a mind of resentment toward sentient beings who are fierce and transgressing the precepts, either abandons them himself or obstructs others from helping them abandon [such behavior], and fails to instruct and transform them, this is called committing many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement."
If one falls into laziness or forgets to prevent [others from wrongdoing], the transgression arises from non-afflictive causes. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva’s compassion toward those who are evil is deeper than that toward those who are virtuous.
There is no offense if one is insane;
or if one knows [the truth] but does not speak it for the purpose of subduing the other person, as previously explained.
If it is to protect the minds of others;
or if it is to protect the regulations of the Sangha.

"If a Bodhisattva, regarding those offenses prohibited by the Tathāgata’s Prātimokṣa and established as *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offenses) within the Vinaya, [abstains from them] for the sake of protecting sentient beings—causing those without faith to have faith and increasing the faith of those who already have—it is the same as training as a Śrāvaka."

Why is this? Śrāvakas, at the very least, seek their own deliverance; they do not fail to protect others by causing those without faith to have faith, and by increasing the faith and training in the precepts of those who already believe—how much more so for a Bodhisattva’s deliverance through the ultimate truth (paramārtha)?

Furthermore, regarding the prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) established by the Blessed One for the sake of the śrāvakas—those who abide in little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means—a bodhisattva does not train in these precepts in the same manner.

Why is this? Because the śrāvaka seeks only his own liberation and abandons others; he should abide in little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means. It is not fitting for the bodhisattva, who liberates both himself and others, to abide in little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means.

For the sake of sentient beings, a bodhisattva may seek hundreds of thousands of robes from Brahmins or householders who are not their relatives; even when these are offered freely, the bodhisattva should observe whether the donor is capable of giving or not, and accept them accordingly.
As it is with robes, so it is with alms bowls.
As it is with robes and alms bowls, so too may one personally solicit thread and have a weaver who is not a relative weave [robes];
for the sake of sentient beings, one should accumulate *kōśeya* (silk) bedding and sitting mats, even up to hundreds or thousands.
Even gold and silver to the extent of hundreds of thousands should likewise be accepted.

In such matters as these, where there is little benefit, little activity, and little application of skillful means, what constitutes an offense for a śrāvaka to avoid is not a point of shared training for a bodhisattva.

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s vows of restraint, if one harbors a mind of resentment toward sentient beings and remains content with little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement.
If one falls into indolence, remaining with little benefit, little activity, and little skillful means, this constitutes an offense arising from non-affliction.

If a bodhisattva is deceitful and crooked in body and speech—whether by manifesting signs, disparaging others, or seeking profit through profit—and dwells in a way of life based on wrong livelihood, lacking a sense of shame and dread of blame, and being unable to abandon such conduct, this is called committing many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction.
There is no offense if, for the sake of severing that [fault], one applies the means with desire, yet due to the predominance of afflictions, it arises again and again.

If a bodhisattva, being agitated and finding no delight in tranquility, makes loud noises and plays for sport so as to bring joy to others, acting on this cause and condition, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
If it is forgotten or done by mistake, the offense is non-afflicted.
There is no offense in cases such as those previously described: when one gives rise to the desire and employs skillful means for the purpose of abandoning that [fault].
Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases:
when another has given rise to resentment and one acts with the desire to cause it to cease;
or when another is afflicted by sorrow and anxiety, and one acts with the desire to cause it to subside.
If others are by nature fond of play, he engages in it for the sake of attracting them, for the sake of severing [their attachment], and for the sake of protecting them;
or if others harbor doubts toward the Bodhisattva, feeling resentment or opposition, he displays a smiling countenance to manifest the purity of his mind.
"If a bodhisattva holds such a view and speaks thus:
'A bodhisattva should not delight in nirvāṇa, but should turn away from nirvāṇa;
one should not fear the afflictions, nor should one be exclusively weary of them.'"
Why is this? A bodhisattva ought to undergo birth and death for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas in order to seek great enlightenment.
To speak in such a manner is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement.

Why is this? Because the śrāvakas’ deep delight in nirvāṇa and their dread and aversion toward afflictions are a hundred thousand million times less than that of the bodhisattvas’ deep delight in nirvāṇa and their dread and aversion toward afflictions.
That is to say, while the śrāvakas act solely for their own benefit, bodhisattvas do not; rather, they act universally for the sake of all sentient beings.
Their practice does not defile the mind, surpassing even that of the arhats;
though they achieve that which is with outflows (sāsrava), they remain free from all afflictions (kleśa).

"If a bodhisattva does not guard against words of lack of faith, does not guard against derision and defamation, and likewise does not eliminate them—if there are actual faults and evils that are not eliminated, this is called committing many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction."
There is indeed no fault or evil that has not been eliminated, nor does it arise from defilement.
There is no offense in the following cases: if non-Buddhists or other wicked persons slander [the teaching]; or...
If one goes forth as a mendicant and cultivates the causes and conditions for goodness, it may give rise to the censure and slander of others;
whether the person before them is angry or insane, they may thus produce such censure and slander.

"If a bodhisattva, observing that sentient beings would benefit from words of harsh admonition through skillful means, fails to provide them out of fear that it will cause them distress and sorrow, this is called committing many offenses; this offense arises from non-afflictive causes."
There is no offense if one observes that the person currently provides little benefit and would instead give rise to much distress.

If a bodhisattva, when reviled, reviles in return; when provoked to anger, returns anger; when struck, strikes back; or when slandered, slanders in return—this is called a transgression of many offenses, and it is a transgression arising from defilement.

"If a bodhisattva offends another, or even if they do not offend but causes another to suspect them, they should immediately repent and apologize. If, out of resentment or contempt, they do not repent and apologize in accordance with the Dharma, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement. If, however, they fail to do so due to indolence or laziness, the transgression arises not from defilement."
There is no offense in the following cases: if one employs skillful means to subdue the other;
or if the other intends to perform an impure act before accepting [the apology], then there is no fault in not apologizing.
If one knows that the other person is by nature fond of quarreling and litigation, then offering an apology will only increase their anger;
if one knows that the other person is harmonious and patient, free from resentment, then failing to apologize out of fear of causing them shame carries no fault.

"If a bodhisattva, when another person comes to them having committed an offense and offers a formal apology and confession according to the Dharma, refuses to accept that confession out of a heart of resentment and with the intent to cause them distress, this is called an offense of many transgressions; it is an offense arising from affliction."
If one does not feel resentment or hatred, yet by nature refuses to accept the confession, this constitutes an offense that arises from non-defilement.
There is no offense in cases where one employs skillful means to bring the other person to subjection, as previously described.
If the other person does not repent according to the Dharma, and their mind remains unpacified such that they do not accept the confession, there is no offense.

However, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of resentment toward another and persists in holding onto it without relinquishing it, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
There is no offense if, for the sake of severing that [affliction], one generates the desire and applies the means as previously described.
"If a bodhisattva, out of a desire for being served, maintains a retinue, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement."
There is no offense if one keeps [possessions] without a mind of greed.

"If a bodhisattva, being indolent and lazy, indulges in the pleasure of sleep, or does so at an improper time or without moderation, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement."
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one lacks strength; if one is exhausted from traveling a great distance;
or if, for the purpose of abandoning that [fault], one applies the means of desire as previously described.
"If a bodhisattva, with a defiled mind, spends time engaging in worldly talk, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from defilement."
If one forgets or errs for a period of time, the offense is non-afflicted.
There is no offense if,
seeing others engaged in conversation, one listens for a brief moment in order to protect their feelings.
If one briefly answers another’s question regarding a matter they have never heard before:

"If a bodhisattva, desiring to seek a concentrated mind, harbors resentment or pride and does not accept the teacher's instruction, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction."
If one falls into indolence through negligence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense if one is ill or lacks physical strength.
If one knows that the person is speaking erroneously;
if one is oneself learned and possesses the necessary capacity;
or if one has already received the Dharma previously.
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to the five hindrances and does not awaken to them, this is called committing a multitude of offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
There is no offense if, for the sake of abandoning them, one generates the desire and applies the means as previously described."
"If a bodhisattva perceives the savoring of dhyāna as a merit, this is called committing a multitude of offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
There is no offense in the following cases:
for the purpose of severing that [savoring], one arouses the desire and applies the means, as previously described."
"If a bodhisattva views things in this way and speaks thus:
'A bodhisattva should not listen to the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas; they should not accept them, nor should they study them.'"
"What use does a bodhisattva have for the teachings of the śrāvakas?
This is called a transgression of many offenses, a transgression arising from affliction. Why is this so?
If a bodhisattva even listens to the heterodox arguments of outsiders, how much more so the words of the Buddha?
There is no offense if one is exclusively studying the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and has not yet been able to master it completely.

"If a bodhisattva does not apply skillful means toward the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, but abandons it and fails to study it, instead practicing exclusively the sūtras and dharmas of the śrāvakas, this is called committing many offenses; this offense arises from non-afflictive causes."

"If a bodhisattva, regarding what has been taught by the Buddha, abandons it and fails to study it, instead practicing the heterodox treatises of external paths or worldly scriptures, this is called committing a multitude of offenses; this offense arises from defilement."
There is no offense in the following cases:
if one is of superior intelligence and is able to learn quickly;
or if, having studied for a long time, one does not forget.
If one contemplates and understands the meaning;
if one thoroughly observes the Buddha-dharma and attains immovable wisdom;
and if, day after day, one studies Buddhist scriptures for two parts of the time and secular texts for one part;
This is called non-offense.

If a bodhisattva is skilled in worldly treatises and the heterodox arguments of outsiders, yet takes pleasure in them, does not abandon them, and does not regard them as poison, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction.

"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing the profound meaning of the Bodhisattva Dharma-piṭaka, its true meaning, and the immeasurable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, slanders them and refuses to accept them, saying:
'These are not beneficial; they were not spoken by the Tathāgata; nor can they bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.'"
This is called committing a multitude of offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
One may slander either due to improper reflection within one's own mind, or by following the lead of others.
When this bodhisattva hears the foremost, most profound meaning, they do not give rise to a mind of understanding.
This bodhisattva should arouse a mind of faith and a mind free from deceit, training themselves in this way:
"I am greatly at fault; I am blind and lack the eye of wisdom."
“The Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom speaks thus in accordance with reality;
since the Tathāgata’s teaching is incomplete [in its literal sense], how can you give rise to slander?
Such a bodhisattva places himself in a position of ignorance.
Thus the Tathāgata, having directly known and seen these dharmas, correctly contemplates and correctly directs them; he does not transgress, nor is he ignorant or slanderous.
"If a bodhisattva, with a mind of greed or anger, praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is called a 'multitudinous offense,' and it is an offense arising from defilement."
There is no offense if one disparages non-Buddhists in order to praise the Buddha-dharma;
or if one employs skillful means to subdue them, as previously described.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases:
[if it is] to cause those without faith to have faith, or to increase and broaden the faith of those who already have it.

"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing that there is a place where the Dharma is being taught or a place for definitive discussion, does not go to listen due to a mind of pride or a mind of resentment, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction."
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense if one does not understand, if one is ill, if one lacks strength, if the other person teaches the Dharma erroneously, or if one protects the mind of the speaker.
If one hears repeatedly, has already received and maintained [the teachings], and knows their meaning;
if one is of great learning, maintains what is heard, or practices according to the teaching;
or if one cultivates meditative concentration without wishing to abandon it even for a moment.
If one is of dull faculties, it is difficult to awaken to, difficult to receive, and difficult to maintain;
for those who do not go [to hear the teaching], there is no offense.

"If a Bodhisattva treats the teacher of the Dharma with contempt, fails to give rise to reverence, mocks or reviles them, and clings only to the literal words rather than relying on the true meaning, this is called a transgression of many offenses, and it is an offense arising from defilement."

"If a bodhisattva, abiding in the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), sees sentient beings engaged in various activities and, out of a mind of malice and resentment, does not join them in their work—namely:

deliberating on various matters, traveling on a journey, engaging in righteous enterprise, farming, herding cattle, mediating disputes, participating in auspicious assemblies, or performing meritorious deeds."
To not join with them is called a "multitudinous offense" (prāyaścittika), and it is an offense arising from defilement.
If one fails to do so due to indolence or laziness, it is an offense arising from non-defilement.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one lacks the strength;
if the other person is able to manage it themselves; if the other person already has many companions; or if the task to be performed is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the righteous purpose.
If one employs skillful means to subdue them as previously described;
or if one has already given a prior promise to another; or if that person harbors resentment;

or if one is practicing wholesome deeds oneself and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment; or if one is by nature dull-witted; or if one seeks to protect the sentiments of many people; or if one seeks to uphold the regulations of the Sangha.
If one does not associate with them, there is no offense in any case.

"If a bodhisattva, seeing a person who is weak and ill, fails to go and visit them out of a mind of anger and resentment, this is called committing a multitude of offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement."
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense if one is personally ill, lacks physical strength, or instructs someone who has the strength to attend to the sick person accordingly.
If one knows that the person has their own attendants, or if they have the capacity to manage [the illness] themselves;
or if the illness recurs frequently, or is chronic;
or if they are engaged in superior practices and do not wish to abandon them even temporarily; [then one should not take charge].
If one is dull-witted, difficult to awaken, difficult to receive [the teaching], difficult to retain, and unable to abide within the conditions;
or if one first attends to the illnesses of others—
just as with illness, so it is with poverty and suffering.

"If a bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings committing evil deeds in this life and future lives, fails to provide correct instruction out of a mind of resentment and hatred, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction."
There is no offense if:
one lacks wisdom oneself; one lacks the power [to speak]; or one causes someone who possesses power to speak;
or if that person possesses power themselves; or if that person possesses good spiritual friends themselves.
If one employs skillful means to subdue them, as previously described;
yet if they harbor hatred toward me when the teaching is correctly explained,
or if they utter harsh words, or if they misunderstand it, or if they lack love and respect, or if that person’s nature is wicked and perverse.

"If a bodhisattva, having received a kindness from another, out of a mind of resentment fails to repay it with an equivalent or greater return, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction."
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-defilement. There is no offense in the following cases:
if one has applied effort but lacks the power; or if one employs a skillful means to subdue the other person, as previously described.
If one wishes to repay a kindness but the other person does not accept it;

or if a bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings facing difficulties regarding relatives or difficulties regarding wealth and property, fails out of a mind of resentment to resolve them or remove their distress—this is called a transgression of many offenses, a transgression arising from defilement.
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense in cases as previously explained regarding different matters.

"If a bodhisattva, when requested for food, drink, or clothing, fails to give them due to a mind of resentment and hatred, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is a transgression arising from affliction."
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense if:
one does not possess [the item] oneself; if one seeks an object that is not in accordance with the Dharma; or if the object would not be beneficial to the recipient.
If one employs skillful means to subdue them as previously described;
or if they have violated the king’s law for the sake of protecting the king's mind;
or if it is to protect the monastic regulations.

"If a bodhisattva gathers a following of disciples and, out of a mind of resentment and hatred, fails to instruct them according to the Dharma, and is unable to seek at appropriate times from brahmins and householders clothing, food, bedding, medicine, and dwellings to provide for them as required—this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from affliction."
If one falls into indolence or negligence, it constitutes an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense if one employs skillful means to subdue the other person, as previously described.
If one is observing the monastic regulations, or is ill, or lacks the strength, one may have someone with strength speak on their behalf;
or if that person has the strength, possesses many acquaintances, and is of great virtue, they may seek the necessary requisites themselves;
or if they have previously received instruction, they already know the Dharma themselves.

If non-Buddhists steal the Dharma and cannot be subdued, and if a bodhisattva, out of a mind of resentment, does not comply with them, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense arising from defilement.
If one falls into indolence, it is an offense arising from non-affliction.
There is no offense if the person intends to perform an improper act.
If one is ill, or lacks strength, or is observing the monastic regulations;
if, although the person acts according to the Dharma, they cause many others to engage in unrighteous conduct;
or for the sake of subduing non-Buddhists, or by means of skillful means to bring them under discipline.
"If a bodhisattva, knowing that other sentient beings possess genuine merit, out of a mind of resentment neither speaks of it to others nor praises it;
and when others do praise them, does not exclaim 'Excellent!'—
this is called committing many offenses, and this offense arises from defilement."
If one falls into indolence or negligence and commits an offense, it arises from non-afflicted motivation.
There is no offense if one knows that the other person has few desires and acts thus to protect their feelings.
If one is ill; if one lacks strength;
if one employs skillful means to subdue that person;
or if one is observing the regulations of the Saṃgha.
If it causes that person to give rise to afflictions, to overflowing joy, to pride, or to what is unbeneficial— [the teaching acts] for the sake of eliminating these various faults;
or if [it presents] actual virtues as appearing to be non-virtues,
or actual well-spoken teachings as appearing to be not well-spoken.
If it is for the purpose of subduing the false views of non-Buddhists;
or if one waits until the teaching is finished.

"If a bodhisattva, seeing sentient beings who should be rebuked, who should be suppressed, or who should be punished and expelled, fails to rebuke them due to a defiled mind; [this is a transgression]."
If one reprimands but does not subdue;
or if one subdues but does not penalize or expel—
this is called an offense of many transgressions, an offense arising from defilement.
If one falls into indolence or negligence, it constitutes an offense arising from non-affliction. There is no offense in the following cases:
if the person is incorrigible, cannot be spoken to, is difficult to instruct, or frequently gives rise to resentment; or if they are beyond treatment.
If one observes that it would cause quarrels, disputes, or contradictions; if there would be mutual litigation;
or if it would lead to a dispute within the Sangha, or to a schism in the Sangha.
If they are not deceitful or crooked and possess a sense of shame and remorse, they will gradually reform themselves.
If a bodhisattva has accomplished various supernormal powers, they should terrify those who ought to be terrified and guide those who ought to be guided.

If, for the sake of causing sentient beings to consume their offerings of faith, one does not use supernormal powers to terrify or guide them toward the path, this is called a transgression of many offenses; it is an offense that arises from non-afflictive causes.
There is no offense in the following cases:

if those sentient beings further give rise to defiled attachment; if they are non-Buddhists who slander the noble ones and have perfected wrong views; or if they are all instances where there is no offense.
This also applies if they have become insane or if their painful sensations are increasing.
“O Great Beings! I have already explained many *duṣkṛta* dharmas; if a bodhisattva violates any one of these dharmas, they should perform the repentance for a *duṣkṛta* offense.”
If one does not repent, it will obstruct the bodhisattva precepts.
Now I ask all you great beings:
Are you pure in this regard?
The third proclamation: "O Great Beings!
Since you remain silent, you are pure in this matter; let it be held thus."

“O Great Beings! I have already explained the four *pārājika* dharmas of a bodhisattva and the numerous *duṣkṛta* dharmas; these are the *vinaya-saṃvara-śīla*, the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*, and the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*, as expounded in the *Mātṛkā* compiled by the World-Honored One Maitreya.”
"These various precepts and dharmas can give rise to the bodhisattva practices and can bring the bodhisattva path to fulfillment. 'O Great Beings!
Those who wish to resolve their minds to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should skillfully protect and uphold them.'"

If one protects and upholds [the Dharma], they will not give rise to the thought that the Semblance Dharma is perishing; they can cause the true meaning of the Semblance Dharma to blaze forth and ensure that the True Dharma never ceases.
Their mind attains right abiding, they spontaneously accomplish the Buddha-dharma, and they teach and transform sentient beings without ever becoming weary.
When wholesome karma is perfected, one will swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood!
— *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Bodhisattva Precepts Manual)
